summary: This note summarizes key episodes of the 2004 United States presidential election between George W. Bush and John Kerry, covering the Democratic primaries, the campaign's national security and 'flip-flopper' themes, the first two presidential debates, the campaign finance effects of the McCain–Feingold Act, the Republican convention and ownership society agenda, and the close outcome hinging on Ohio. It also notes how Kerry's campaign survived early trouble through Ted Kennedy's assistance and his own loan to the campaign.
one_line: Overview of the 2004 U.S. presidential election between Bush and Kerry, covering primaries, debates, campaign finance, and the decisive Ohio result.
key_facts: Kerry won the California, Connecticut, Georgia, Maryland, Massachusetts, New York, Ohio, and Rhode Island primaries and the Minnesota caucuses on Super Tuesday in March.
Edwards withdrew from the presidential race after failing to win any state other than South Carolina.
The first debate was held on September 30 at the University of Miami, moderated by Jim Lehrer of PBS.
Bush replied to Kerry's claim about allies in Iraq by saying, "Well, actually, he forgot Poland."
The second presidential debate was held at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri, on October 8, moderated by Charles Gibson of ABC.
Bush joked during the second debate, "That answer made me want to scowl," to address criticism of his scowling demeanor in the first debate.
Bush had established a lead of around 130,000 votes in Ohio on the morning after the election.
Ohio's Secretary of State, Ken Blackwell, announced that it was statistically impossible for Democrats to make up enough valid provisional votes to win, after which Kerry conceded.
Had Kerry won Ohio, he would have won the election despite losing the national popular vote by over 3 million votes.
Bush won the 2000 presidency despite losing the popular vote to Al Gore by over 500,000 votes.
A 269–269 Electoral College tie would have sent the election to the House of Representatives, where each state casts one vote.
Bush officially clinched the number of delegates needed for nomination on March 10, 2004.
Bush accepted the nomination on September 2, 2004, and selected Vice President Dick Cheney as his running mate.

The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002, also known as the McCain–Feingold Bill, was the first campaign finance reform to affect an election, leading to many 527 groups such as Swift Boat Veterans for Truth and MoveOn.org.
Kerry's campaign survived early trouble after Ted Kennedy assigned Mary Beth Cahill as campaign manager and Kerry mortgaged his own home to lend money to the campaign.
